topics.name: Glaciers
topics.kicker: Earth Science concept · Slow-moving rivers of ice that carve mountains
topics.dates: Form over centuries · covered far more of Earth during past ice ages
topics.briefing: A glacier starts out as ordinary snow that never fully melts, year after year, until its own weight presses it into solid, flowing ice. These rivers of ice carved the fjords of Norway and the U-shaped valleys of places like Yosemite, dropping boulders and gravel called moraines wherever they travel. Today almost seventy percent of Earth’s fresh water is locked up inside them, and climate change is causing most of them to shrink.

media.title: Earth Science for Kids: Glaciers
media.note: Quick read: how glaciers form, valley vs. polar glaciers, fjords and moraines, plus a 10-question quiz

qb.tip: Every single one of the 11 real tossups mentions moraines, and most mention calving into icebergs — those are the two clues to drill first. Don’t confuse this answer with icebergs themselves, which are only the floating chunks that break off.

sample.note: the 11 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: These objects grind bedrock into fine “rock flour” and crack into unstable towers of ice called seracs under their own internal stress. They gain mass in an upper “accumulation zone” and lose it in a lower “ablation zone,” where melting finally wins out.
tossups.r: As they move, they pile up ridges of rock and debris, called till, into landforms known as moraines along their edges. For 10 points, name these large, slow-moving masses of land ice.

tossups.p: The surfaces of these objects can show alternating light and dark stripes called ogives, which form as the ice flows through steep icefalls. Alaska’s Malaspina, the largest example of a “piedmont” type, formed where several of these objects merged together.
tossups.r: They break apart at their edges in a process called calving, which creates icebergs. For 10 points, name these objects that hold roughly seventy percent of Earth’s fresh water.

tossups.p: The nineteenth-century Scottish scientist James Forbes pioneered the study of how these objects flow, a movement that speeds up when meltwater beneath them reduces friction with the ground below. Erosion by these objects carves out bowl-shaped hollows called cirques.
tossups.r: Those hollows are separated from each other by razor-thin ridges called aretes. For 10 points, name these large, slow-moving masses of land ice that form from compacted snow.

tossups.p: As they retreat, these objects leave behind streamlined, egg-shaped hills called drumlins and long, winding ridges called eskers made of sorted sand and gravel. They pile rock debris into ridges called moraines along their edges and at their farthest advance.
tossups.r: They come in two main types: smaller ones that flow down mountain valleys, and continental-scale sheets that bury whole landmasses like Antarctica. For 10 points, a National Park in Montana takes its very name from what large masses of moving ice?

tossups.p: Small mountain lakes called tarns can form when meltwater fills the bowl-shaped hollows these objects carve. Surface meltwater on these objects plunges downward through vertical shafts called moulins, sometimes reaching all the way to the base.
tossups.r: As they melted back at the end of the last ice age, they helped carve out the basins that became the Great Lakes. For 10 points, name these huge, moving bodies of ice.

tossups.p: Iceland’s Okjökull [“OH-kyer-kootl”] lost its official status as one of these objects in 2014 and was memorialized five years later with a plaque whose inscription ends “Only you know if we did it.” Many of these objects have lost mass almost every single year since the late 1980s as the climate has warmed.
tossups.r: Moving ice within them can crack open deep fissures called crevasses. For 10 points, name these large, slow-moving masses of land ice.

tossups.p: Internal stress on these objects can crack their surfaces into towers of ice called seracs, while their grinding motion pulverizes stone into a fine powder called rock flour. Debris carried along by these objects settles into ridges called moraines when the ice melts back.
tossups.r: Chunks that break off the edges of these objects in a process called calving become icebergs. For 10 points, name these objects that hold about seventy percent of the planet’s fresh water.

tossups.p: These objects gain mass where snowfall outpaces melting, in a zone called the accumulation zone, and lose mass in the opposite ablation zone. Their flow, studied by the pioneering scientist James Forbes, speeds up through a kind of sliding that occurs when meltwater at their base reduces friction with the ground.
tossups.r: Their erosion carves out deep U-shaped valleys, which flood with seawater along mountainous coastlines to form fjords. For 10 points, name these objects formed when layers of snow compact into ice over many years.

tossups.p: Alternating bands of light and dark ice, called ogives, appear on the surfaces of these objects as they flow through steep sections called icefalls. As they retreat, these objects leave streamlined hills called drumlins and sinuous ridges of gravel called eskers behind them.
tossups.r: They exist in two main forms: smaller ones confined to mountain valleys, and vast continental-scale sheets that bury whole landmasses like Greenland. For 10 points, as they melted at the end of the last ice age, what large masses of ice helped carve out the Great Lakes?

tossups.p: Alaska’s Malaspina, the largest “piedmont” example of one of these objects, formed from the merger of several smaller ones. Hollowed-out basins left behind by these objects often fill with meltwater to become small lakes called tarns.
tossups.r: Surface meltwater on top of these objects can plunge downward through narrow vertical shafts called moulins. For 10 points, a Montana National Park is named directly for what large, slow-moving masses of ice?

tossups.p: As they pile up rock and debris called till into ridges called moraines, these objects also grind stone into fine “rock flour.” Internal stress within these objects can crack their surfaces into unstable towers of ice called seracs.
tossups.r: Moving ice inside them can also split open deep cracks called crevasses. For 10 points, name these large, slow-moving masses of land ice.

tossups.p: The Scottish scientist James Forbes studied how these objects flow, a movement that speeds up when meltwater beneath them reduces friction with the ground below. Iceland’s Okjökull lost its official status as one of these objects in 2014, later memorialized with a plaque.
tossups.r: Pieces that break off the front edges of these objects in a process called calving become icebergs floating at sea. For 10 points, name these objects that hold roughly seventy percent of Earth’s fresh water.

tossups.p: Erosion from these objects carves bowl-shaped hollows called cirques, separated from one another by razor-thin ridges called aretes. Alternating light and dark stripes called ogives can appear on the surfaces of these objects as they flow through steep icefalls.
tossups.r: They form in the first place when layers of snow pile up faster than they can melt, compacting over many years into dense ice. For 10 points, name these objects that form from compacted snow.

tossups.p: As they retreat, these objects leave behind streamlined, egg-shaped hills called drumlins and long, winding ridges of sand and gravel called eskers. They also gain mass in an accumulation zone and lose mass in an ablation zone further down their length.
tossups.r: Deep U-shaped valleys carved by these objects can flood with seawater along mountainous coasts to form fjords. For 10 points, name these objects whose melting at the end of the last ice age helped carve out North America’s Great Lakes.

tossups.p: Small mountain lakes called tarns can form when meltwater fills bowl-shaped hollows left behind by these objects. Alaska’s Malaspina, the largest “piedmont” example of one of these objects, formed where several smaller ones merged together, and moving ice within them can crack open deep fissures called crevasses.
tossups.r: Most of these objects, tracked yearly by scientists, have lost mass almost every year since the late 1980s as the climate has warmed. For 10 points, a Montana National Park is named for what masses of moving ice, which hold about seventy percent of Earth’s fresh water?

trap.title: Glaciers, or just icebergs?
trap.body: Most real tossups eventually mention calving, the process by which icebergs break off a glacier’s edge into the water. Hearing “ice,” “ocean,” and “breaking apart” together tempts some players to blurt out icebergs — but an iceberg is only the floating piece that calved away, not the slow-moving mass of land ice the rest of the clues describe.
trap.fix: Icebergs are a RESULT of glaciers, not glaciers themselves. If the clues describe movement, moraines, crevasses, or valleys carved over a long time, the answer is glaciers; save “iceberg” for a clue that is only about the floating piece after it breaks off.
trap.line: Real answer line: glaciers [accept ice sheet or ice shelf].

topics.name: Quartz
topics.kicker: Common silicate mineral · Its vibrations keep time in clocks and watches
topics.briefing: Quartz is one of the most common minerals on Earth, built from nothing more than silicon and oxygen locked into a six-sided crystal. Squeeze a piece of it and it makes a tiny electric charge, a trick called piezoelectricity that keeps your watch ticking and your phone’s clock accurate. Purple amethyst, yellow citrine, and pink rose quartz are all this exact same mineral, just tinted by trace impurities.

media.title: Quartz Facts for Kids
media.note: Quick read: silicon dioxide (SiO₂), hardness 7 on the Mohs scale, piezoelectricity, and amethyst and citrine

qb.tip: Only 3 Middle School/Easy High School tossups exist, but they (and 9 Regular HS ones) agree closely: Mohs 7, piezoelectricity, Bowen’s reaction series, and “shocked” quartz are in most of them.

sample.note: the 12 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (3 Middle School/Easy High School + 9 Regular High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: Nicolas Steno’s observation that this mineral’s crystal faces always meet at a 60-degree angle helped found the science of crystallography. Along with iridium, a “shocked” form of this mineral found at the Chicxulub [“CHEEK-shoo-loob”] crater supports the Alvarez hypothesis for the extinction of the dinosaurs.
tossups.r: This mineral sits at the very bottom of Bowen’s reaction series, so it is usually the last to crystallize out of cooling magma. For 10 points, name this silicate mineral with the chemical formula SiO2, which defines the number 7 on the Mohs hardness scale.

tossups.p: A fused, glassy form of this mineral was shaped into some of the most nearly perfect spheres ever manufactured, used as gyroscope rotors on NASA’s Gravity Probe B satellite. This mineral is used in the Pierce oscillator circuit because squeezing it produces a voltage.
tossups.r: That property, piezoelectricity, is why slices of this mineral keep clocks and watches ticking at a precise rate. For 10 points, name this mineral, the second most abundant in Earth’s crust after feldspar.

tossups.p: This mineral is extremely resistant to chemical weathering, which places it at the bottom of the Goldich dissolution series. A reddish-brown variety of this mineral that shimmers with an optical effect called chatoyancy [“shuh-TOY-un-see”] is sold as Tiger’s Eye.
tossups.r: Rare, double-terminated crystals of this mineral found in upstate New York are nicknamed “Herkimer diamonds.” For 10 points, name this mineral that forms purple amethyst and yellow citrine when colored by trace impurities.

tossups.p: Above about 573 degrees Celsius, this mineral flips into a different hexagonal “beta” crystal form. This mineral is built from a repeating three-dimensional framework of tetrahedra, each with one silicon atom bonded to four oxygen atoms that link to neighboring units.
tossups.r: This mineral typically grows as a six-sided prism that tapers to a point. For 10 points, name this silicate mineral with the formula SiO2, which is the main ingredient of most sand and sandstone.

tossups.p: A green, mica-flecked variety of this mineral is called aventurine, while a crystal with both orange and purple sections is called ametrine. This mineral lacks true cleavage, so it breaks instead with a smooth, curved conchoidal fracture.
tossups.r: This mineral is often found paired with feldspar inside granite. For 10 points, name this mineral with a Mohs hardness of 7, whose colored varieties include amethyst, citrine, and a pink form.

tossups.p: Besides keeping time, this mineral’s piezoelectric effect also makes it useful in microphones, sonar devices, and ultrasound transducers. A “shocked” variety of this mineral forms under the extreme pressure of a meteorite impact or an underground nuclear test.
tossups.r: This mineral has the lowest crystallization temperature of any common silicate, landing it at the bottom of Bowen’s reaction series. For 10 points, name this mineral with chemical formula SiO2 and a hardness of 7 on the Mohs scale.

tossups.p: A “fused” form of this mineral, melted and cooled into a non-crystalline glass, is prized for fiber-optic cable and laboratory glassware because it resists heat and lets ultraviolet light through. This mineral crystallizes in the trigonal system, often forming hexagonal prisms.
tossups.r: Squeezing this mineral generates a small electric charge, a property called piezoelectricity. For 10 points, name this mineral found in granite and sandstone, the second most abundant mineral in Earth’s crust.

tossups.p: In the Alvarez hypothesis, a “shocked” form of this mineral found in rock layers worldwide supports the theory that an asteroid impact ended the age of dinosaurs. Friedrich Mohs chose this mineral to define the number 7 on his 10-point hardness scale.
tossups.r: Clocks and watches use thin slices of this mineral because pressing on it produces a tiny voltage. For 10 points, name this mineral with formula SiO2, whose colored varieties include purple amethyst and a pink form.

tossups.p: This mineral’s resistance to weathering places it at the bottom of the Goldich dissolution series, the opposite end from easily weathered minerals like olivine. Rare crystals of this mineral with points on both ends, found near a town in New York State, are nicknamed “Herkimer diamonds.”
tossups.r: This mineral’s piezoelectric property makes it vibrate at a precise frequency when a voltage is applied. For 10 points, name this mineral with a Mohs hardness of 7, the main component of beach sand.

tossups.p: This mineral is the last to crystallize on both branches of Bowen’s reaction series, after minerals like olivine and feldspar have already solidified. Nicolas Steno noticed that no matter the size of this mineral’s crystals, their faces always meet at the same 60-degree angle.
tossups.r: Besides its clear, colorless form, this mineral’s varieties include purple amethyst and yellow citrine. For 10 points, name this silicate mineral with formula SiO2 and a Mohs hardness of 7.

tossups.p: A “shocked” variety of this mineral, formed by extreme pressure, turns up both at meteorite impact craters and at sites of underground nuclear testing. This mineral’s crystal structure gives way to a different, hexagonal “beta” form above 573 degrees Celsius.
tossups.r: Pressing on this mineral produces a small voltage, a property that helps wristwatches keep accurate time. For 10 points, name this mineral, the second most abundant in Earth’s crust behind feldspar.

tossups.p: This mineral generates a voltage when placed under stress, a property used in the Pierce oscillator and in ultrasound machines. Because it is nearly the last mineral to solidify from cooling magma, this mineral sits at the bottom of Bowen’s reaction series.
tossups.r: A melted, “fused” form of this mineral is spun into fiber-optic cable. For 10 points, name this mineral that registers 7 on the Mohs hardness scale and forms six-sided crystals with the chemical formula SiO2.

tossups.p: Along with iridium, a “shocked” form of this mineral at the Chicxulub crater is cited as evidence for the Alvarez hypothesis about the dinosaurs’ extinction. This mineral’s crystal faces were shown by Nicolas Steno to always meet at a 60-degree angle, regardless of the crystal’s overall shape.
tossups.r: This mineral is extremely resistant to weathering, landing it at the bottom of the Goldich dissolution series. For 10 points, name this mineral whose colored varieties include amethyst, citrine, and a pink form.

tossups.p: This mineral’s piezoelectric effect means it vibrates at an exact, steady rate when a small voltage is applied, which is why it regulates the timing in digital clocks, watches, and radios. A fused, glassy version of this mineral was ground into gyroscope rotors for NASA’s Gravity Probe B.
tossups.r: This mineral commonly forms six-sided prism crystals and comes in colored varieties like smoky, rose, and milky. For 10 points, name this mineral with chemical formula SiO2, defined as a 7 on the Mohs hardness scale.

tossups.p: This mineral is built from repeating units of one silicon atom bonded to four oxygen atoms, with those units linking into a three-dimensional framework with the overall ratio of one silicon to two oxygens. It is found at the very bottom of both Bowen’s reaction series and the Goldich dissolution series.
tossups.r: Granite gets its glassy-looking grains from this mineral, and most of its other grains from feldspar. For 10 points, name this mineral with formula SiO2, whose piezoelectric property makes it useful in clocks and watches.

Defines the number 7 on the 10-point Mohs hardness scale
Piezoelectric: makes a tiny electric charge under pressure, which keeps clocks and watches accurate
Colored varieties include purple amethyst, yellow citrine, and a pink form called rose
Second most abundant mineral in Earth’s crust, just behind feldspar
Sits at the bottom of Bowen’s reaction series, the last common mineral to crystallize from cooling magma
A “shocked” form forms under extreme pressure, such as a meteorite impact or an underground nuclear test
Main mineral in sand and sandstone; paired with feldspar inside granite
Extremely resistant to chemical weathering, landing it at the bottom of the Goldich dissolution series
Crystallizes in the trigonal system, usually as a six-sided hexagonal prism
A reddish-brown variety called Tiger’s Eye shimmers with an optical effect called chatoyancy
A melted, “fused” glassy form is used in fiber-optic cable and lab glassware
Rare double-terminated clear crystals from New York are nicknamed “Herkimer diamonds”
A shocked form plus iridium at the Chicxulub crater supports the Alvarez hypothesis for the dinosaurs’ extinction
Nicolas Steno found that its crystal faces always meet at a 60-degree angle, no matter the crystal’s size
Used in the Pierce oscillator circuit, where its vibration keeps an electronic frequency steady
Transforms into a different hexagonal “beta” crystal form above about 573 degrees Celsius
A fused form was shaped into near-perfectly round gyroscope spheres for NASA’s Gravity Probe B satellite
Lacks true cleavage planes, so it breaks instead with a smooth, curved conchoidal fracture
Can grow as a single bicolor crystal, half orange and half purple, called ametrine
A green variety flecked with tiny mica crystals is called aventurine
Its piezoelectric effect is also used in microphones, sonar, and medical ultrasound devices
Built from a 3-D framework of tetrahedra, each a silicon atom bonded to four oxygen atoms shared with neighbors

trap.title: Mineral, or just a color?
trap.body: Amethyst, citrine, and rose quartz are not separate minerals — they are this exact same mineral, tinted by trace impurities. But on a real tossup, naming the color variety instead of the mineral itself is a different, more specific answer and is marked wrong. The same goes for quartzite, which is a metamorphic rock made mostly of this mineral, not the mineral itself, and for feldspar, the only mineral more abundant in Earth’s crust.
trap.fix: If the clues mention a specific color name (amethyst, citrine, rose, smoky) without ever naming the general mineral, wait for a clue that is true of all of them, like the Mohs hardness of 7 or the SiO2 formula, before you buzz with the general name.
trap.line: Real answer line: Quartz (accept shocked quartz; prompt on silica or silicon dioxide).

topics.name: Hurricanes
topics.kicker: Giant rotating tropical storms · Run on warm ocean water, not gasoline
topics.briefing: A hurricane is like an engine that burns warm ocean water instead of gasoline. Moist air rises and spins into a wheel of thunderstorms hundreds of miles wide, with a strangely calm “eye” at the center ringed by its most violent winds, the eyewall. Scientists rank these storms on the five-step Saffir-Simpson scale, and the names of the worst ones, like Katrina and Harvey, get retired for good.

media.note: Quick read: how hurricanes form, the eye and eye wall, categories, and naming, plus a 10-question quiz

qb.tip: Two of the seven results, Hurricane Katrina and Hurricane Harvey, are about one specific storm, not the general phenomenon — that mismatch is the Buzzer Trap below.

sample.note: 5 of the 7 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (the other 2 named one specific storm instead; Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: The Fujiwhara [“foo-jee-WAH-rah”] Effect describes how two of these systems can interact or merge. Size can be measured by the ROCI, or “radius of outermost closed isobar.” A “stadium effect,” an inverted dome shape, can appear around the calm center of a strong one of these systems.
tossups.r: The Coriolis effect gives these systems their spin, which is why they almost never form within about 5 degrees of the equator. Wind speed in these storms is ranked on the Saffir-Simpson scale up to Category 5. For 10 points, name these giant rotating tropical storms.

tossups.p: Specialized aircraft nicknamed “Hunters,” including the Lockheed WP-3D Orion, fly directly into these systems to gather data. Climatologist Kerry Emanuel has tracked a decades-long rise in these systems’ destructive force using a “power dissipation index.”
tossups.r: The ring of intense wind and rain surrounding the calm center of these systems is called the eyewall. For 10 points, name these rotating storms rated on the Saffir-Simpson scale, which officially form once sustained winds reach 74 miles per hour.

tossups.p: Forecasters have used the “Mariners’ 1-2-3 Rule” to estimate how far off their predicted path for one of these systems might be. These systems draw their energy from the heat released as warm ocean water evaporates and then condenses inside the storm.
tossups.r: These storms weaken quickly once they make landfall, because crossing onto land cuts off their fuel supply of warm water. For 10 points, name these storms, rated up to Category 5 on the Saffir-Simpson scale, with calm centers called eyes.

tossups.p: The World Meteorological Organization maintains the rotating, alternating-gender lists of names given to these storms, and retires the name of any especially destructive one. These systems can merge through the Fujiwhara Effect, and their size can be described using the ROCI measurement.
tossups.r: Spiral rainbands of thunderstorms wind outward from these systems’ eyewalls. For 10 points, name these giant storms, including examples like Harvey and Maria, which are rated on the five-category Saffir-Simpson scale.

tossups.p: This weather system’s outermost size can be measured by its ROCI, and two of these systems can merge through the Fujiwhara Effect. An inverted-dome “stadium effect” can form around this system’s calm center in its most intense stage.
tossups.r: This system’s worst damage often comes from a storm surge, a wind-driven wall of ocean water pushed onto land. For 10 points, name this type of rotating tropical storm, called a typhoon in the western Pacific, rated on the Saffir-Simpson scale.

tossups.p: Sustained winds of at least 157 miles per hour are needed for one of these systems to reach Category 5, the top of the Saffir-Simpson scale. The Lockheed WP-3D Orion aircraft, nicknamed a “Hunter” of these systems, flies directly into them to collect data.
tossups.r: A ring called the eyewall, which surrounds the calm central eye, drives the worst storm surge onto land. For 10 points, name these giant rotating storms that form over warm tropical oceans and are rated up to Category 5.

tossups.p: Because the Coriolis effect is too weak near the equator, these systems almost never form within about 5 degrees of it. Kerry Emanuel’s “power dissipation index” tracks how the destructive energy of these systems has changed over several decades.
tossups.r: The deadliest part of one of these storms making landfall is often not the wind but the storm surge. For 10 points, name these tropical weather systems, with calm eyes at their centers, rated on the Saffir-Simpson scale.

tossups.p: These storms lent their name to sports teams such as the Carolina team in the NHL and the University of Miami’s teams. The World Meteorological Organization is responsible for retiring the names of the most destructive examples of these systems, such as Harvey and Maria.
tossups.r: These storms grow from a tropical depression into a named tropical storm before finally earning this title once winds reach 74 miles per hour. For 10 points, name these storms with calm eyes, rated on the five-step Saffir-Simpson scale.

tossups.p: The “stadium effect,” in which the clouds of the eyewall lean outward like the seating in a sports arena, can be seen around the center of an especially intense one of these systems. Two of these systems can interact through the Fujiwhara Effect, sometimes merging into one.
tossups.r: The Saffir-Simpson scale ranks these storms by sustained wind speed, from Category 1 up to Category 5. For 10 points, name these giant rotating ocean storms with calm centers called eyes.

tossups.p: This system’s overall size is sometimes described using the ROCI, or radius of its outermost closed isobar. This system forms its spin thanks to the Coriolis effect, which also explains why it almost never forms close to the equator.
tossups.r: In the western Pacific, this same kind of storm is instead called a typhoon. For 10 points, name this type of giant rotating tropical storm, rated on the Saffir-Simpson scale, with a calm “eye” at its center.

tossups.p: The destructive power of these storms over several decades was tracked by Kerry Emanuel using a measurement called the “power dissipation index.” Forecasters have historically used the “Mariners’ 1-2-3 Rule” to budget for error in these systems’ predicted paths.
tossups.r: Named examples of these systems include Katrina, Sandy, and Joaquin. For 10 points, name these rotating tropical storms with sustained winds of at least 74 miles per hour, rated on the Saffir-Simpson scale, with calm eyes at their centers.

tossups.p: A ring of the most violent wind and rain, called the eyewall, surrounds this system’s deceptively calm center. This system is fueled by heat released as warm ocean water evaporates and condenses, which is why it weakens quickly after moving over land or cooler water.
tossups.r: The Saffir-Simpson scale rates this type of storm from Category 1 to Category 5. For 10 points, name this type of giant rotating storm that forms over warm tropical oceans, with examples named from a rotating list maintained by the World Meteorological Organization.

tossups.p: Two of these systems merging is described by the Fujiwhara Effect, and an inverted-dome cloud shape called the “stadium effect” can appear around an intense one’s calm center. These systems almost never form within about 5 degrees of the equator because the Coriolis effect is too weak there.
tossups.r: The Atlantic season for these storms runs from June through November, peaking in September. For 10 points, name these giant storms rated on the Saffir-Simpson scale, which take their energy from warm ocean water.

tossups.p: The ROCI measurement describes this system’s overall size, while the Saffir-Simpson scale describes its intensity. A storm surge, a wind-driven rise in sea level, is often the most destructive part of this weather system’s landfall.
tossups.r: This system’s calm, clear center is surrounded by a ring of violent wind called the eyewall. For 10 points, name this type of giant rotating tropical storm, whose especially destructive examples have their names retired.

tossups.p: This weather system forms in stages, starting as a tropical depression and becoming a named tropical storm before earning this title at 74 miles per hour. Two of these systems can merge through the Fujiwhara Effect, and an intense one can develop a “stadium effect” cloud shape.
tossups.r: This system’s spin comes from the Coriolis effect, and it is rated up to Category 5 on the Saffir-Simpson scale. For 10 points, name this type of giant tropical storm with a calm eye, called a typhoon in the western Pacific.

clues.t: Rated on the five-category Saffir-Simpson scale, from Category 1 up to Category 5
Has a calm, clear “eye” at its center
Forms only over warm tropical ocean water, which fuels the storm with energy

topics.briefing: A tornado is a rope or wedge of furiously spinning air that reaches down from a thunderstorm cloud to touch the ground, and it carries the fastest winds found anywhere on Earth. topics.dates: A constant process, studied scientifically since the 1800s
topics.briefing: Right now, somewhere on Earth, the ground is shaking: tectonic plates grinding past each other release stress that rockets outward as seismic waves. Nearly two thousand years ago, the Chinese inventor Zhang Heng built a bronze device that dropped a ball from a dragon’s mouth to signal that one of these events had struck far away. Today scientists track an event’s P-waves and S-waves to pinpoint its epicenter and measure its magnitude.

sample.note: the 6 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: The Flinn-Engdahl system divides this phenomenon’s occurrences into 754 numbered regions, and elastic rebound theory explains how rock stores and then suddenly releases strain energy to produce one of these events. Multiplying roughly 8.4 by the lag time between two kinds of waves can estimate the distance to this event’s epicenter.
tossups.r: Soil liquefaction, which turns loose ground into quicksand, often accompanies these events along strike-slip faults like California’s San Andreas. For 10 points, name these violent shaking events caused by the sudden release of energy along a fault.

tossups.p: The Mercalli [“mer-KAH-lee”] scale ranks one of these events by the intensity of damage it causes at a given spot, while a separate scale measures the magnitude released at its source. Seismologists increasingly favor a moment magnitude scale over that older scale for very large versions of this event, since the older scale loses accuracy above about magnitude 7.
tossups.r: When one of these events strikes beneath the ocean floor, it can displace enough water to generate a tsunami. For 10 points, name this sudden shaking of the ground, often measured on the Richter scale.

tossups.p: In 132 CE, the Chinese polymath Zhang Heng built an early detector for this phenomenon, a bronze vessel whose dragon heads dropped a ball whenever one of these events struck far away. Elastic rebound theory describes how rock stores and then suddenly releases strain energy to produce this kind of event.
tossups.r: Instruments called seismographs record this event’s primary and secondary waves, abbreviated P-waves and S-waves. For 10 points, name this sudden release of energy that shakes the ground, often along a fault.

tossups.p: This phenomenon’s underground point of origin is called its focus or hypocenter, while the point directly above it on the surface is its epicenter. These events cluster most heavily along the boundaries of tectonic plates, where stress built up along a fault is suddenly released.
tossups.r: A smaller event of the same kind, called an aftershock, often follows the largest shock in a sequence. For 10 points, name this violent shaking of the ground.

tossups.p: Surface waves named for Augustus Love and Lord Rayleigh travel along the surface of the ground during one of these events. In loose, waterlogged soil, this kind of event can trigger liquefaction, turning solid-seeming ground into a quicksand-like slurry. Injecting oil-field wastewater deep underground has made smaller versions of this event more common in the central United States.
tossups.r: Even so, the strongest versions of this event in the United States still strike most often along the Pacific coast. For 10 points, name this sudden shaking of the ground.

tossups.p: Seismic stations on the far side of Earth from one of these events fail to receive the secondary waves it produces; that gap, called a shadow zone, gave scientists some of the first solid evidence that part of Earth’s core is liquid.
tossups.r: In 1975, Chinese scientists successfully predicted a destructive version of this event near Haicheng based on changes in groundwater and animal behavior. For 10 points, name this violent shaking of the ground.

tossups.p: A strike-slip fault like California’s San Andreas is a common setting for one of these events, which begins at an underground focus before stress-release waves spread outward toward the surface. Timing the delay between an event’s first two wave arrivals gives seismologists a rough distance to its point of origin.
tossups.r: Instruments called seismometers record this event’s magnitude on a logarithmic scale. For 10 points, name this sudden shaking caused by the release of built-up tectonic stress.

tossups.p: Rock on either side of a locked fault bends and stores elastic energy for years before suddenly snapping back toward its original shape, a process that explains why one of these events occurs where it does. The sudden slip that results sends seismic waves outward in all directions from the point of rupture.
tossups.r: Large versions of this event are often followed by a series of smaller aftershocks along the same fault. For 10 points, name this sudden release of stored energy that shakes the ground.

tossups.p: One widely used scale for this phenomenon measures the felt intensity of shaking at a given location, while a different scale instead estimates the total energy released at the source. Because that energy-based scale becomes unreliable for the very largest versions of this event, seismologists today more often report a moment magnitude instead.
tossups.r: A great many of these events strike along the Pacific Ring of Fire. For 10 points, name this natural disaster that shakes the ground, which can be measured on the Richter scale.

tossups.p: When one of these events occurs on the ocean floor along a subduction zone, it can displace a huge column of water and set off a tsunami. Stress can build for decades along the boundary between two tectonic plates before this kind of event suddenly releases it as seismic waves.
tossups.r: Seismologists study the slow motion of the Earth’s crust to help forecast where this kind of event is most likely to strike next. For 10 points, name this sudden shaking of the ground.

tossups.p: Buildings built on loose, waterlogged soil are especially at risk when one of these events causes liquefaction, a process that turns firm-seeming ground into a flowing slurry. Rolling surface waves, including Rayleigh waves, can sometimes be seen moving across open ground during a strong version of this event.
tossups.r: These events happen most often at or near fault lines, where tectonic plates meet. For 10 points, name this sudden violent shaking of the ground.

tossups.p: Long before modern instruments existed, the Han-dynasty inventor Zhang Heng built a bronze device that used a dropped ball to signal the direction of one of these events nearly two thousand years ago. Modern seismographs instead record this event’s faster primary waves and slower secondary waves to calculate how far away it struck.
tossups.r: Scientists call the underground point where this event begins its focus, and the point on the surface directly above it the epicenter. For 10 points, name this sudden, violent shaking of the ground.

tossups.p: Seismologists Flinn and Engdahl divided the globe into 754 numbered regions still used today to catalog where one of these events strikes. Analysts can estimate how far away this kind of event occurred by timing the gap between the arrival of its two main wave types.
tossups.r: Most of these events are too small to be felt, but the largest can severely damage buildings and bridges in seconds. For 10 points, name this sudden shaking of the ground along a fault.

tossups.p: Tectonic plates sliding past, toward, or away from each other store enormous stress along the faults where they meet, and this kind of event is how that stress finally releases. Scientists now prefer the moment magnitude scale over the older Richter scale when measuring this event’s very largest examples.
tossups.r: Giant versions of this event beneath the ocean can trigger tsunamis that cross entire oceans. For 10 points, name this sudden shaking of the ground.

tossups.p: Scientists called seismologists study this phenomenon by analyzing the P-waves and S-waves recorded on a seismograph. The point on Earth’s surface directly above where this event begins underground is called its epicenter, and the event’s strength is often reported on the Richter scale.
tossups.r: This kind of event is caused by the sudden movement of rock along a fault, often where two tectonic plates meet. For 10 points, name this natural disaster in which the ground suddenly shakes.

trap.title: Earthquake, aftershock, or tsunami?
trap.body: Earthquakes, aftershocks, and tsunamis are easy to mix up because one often causes the next: a big earthquake under the ocean can trigger a tsunami, and a large earthquake is almost always followed by smaller aftershocks along the same fault. Clues about the ground shaking, fault lines, and seismographs point to the main event itself, not its aftereffects.
trap.fix: If the clue is about a wave of water flooding a coastline, the answer is tsunami. If it is about a smaller, later tremor along the same fault, the answer is aftershock. If it is about rock suddenly slipping along a fault and the ground shaking, say earthquake.

topics.name: Mantle
topics.kicker: Thick rock layer between crust and core · Its slow flow drives plate tectonics
topics.dates: Formed along with the rest of Earth, about 4.5 billion years ago
topics.briefing: Beneath your feet lies a layer of hot, slowly flowing rock that makes up 84 percent of Earth’s entire volume. Though it is solid rock, it behaves like an extremely thick liquid over millions of years, churning in massive convection currents that drag the crustal plates above it across the planet. No drilling project, including one by a Japanese research ship, has ever managed to bore all the way down to it.

sample.note: the 7 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: A mineral called post-perovskite is thought to exist near the bottom 200 kilometers of this region, a zone nicknamed D double-prime that sits just above the Gutenberg discontinuity. The upper part of this region, by contrast, is especially rich in the mineral olivine.
tossups.r: Magnesium oxide is the second most abundant compound in this mostly solid, slowly flowing layer. For 10 points, name this huge rock layer of Earth that lies between the crust and the core.

tossups.p: The Japanese research vessel Chikyu has attempted to drill a borehole deep enough to sample this region directly, though no project has ever succeeded. Just below the crust, the upper part of this region contains a low-velocity zone where seismic waves travel more slowly than usual.
tossups.r: Convection currents within this region are the engine that drives the slow motion of tectonic plates above it. For 10 points, name this thick layer of hot rock that makes up most of Earth’s volume.

tossups.p: The Mohorovičić [“moh-ho-ROH-vih-chich”] discontinuity marks this region’s upper edge, just beneath Earth’s crust. Its plastic, slow-flowing upper portion, the asthenosphere, lies beneath a rigid cap called the lithosphere, which also includes the crust and the very topmost sliver of this region.
tossups.r: Though technically solid rock, it behaves like an extremely thick liquid over millions of years. For 10 points, name this layer of Earth sandwiched between the crust and the core.

tossups.p: The lowest part of this region is called D double-prime, and the Lehmann [“LAY-mun”] discontinuity marks an abrupt jump in seismic wave speed within its low-velocity zone beneath continents. Convection currents churning through this layer are what drag Earth’s tectonic plates across the surface.
tossups.r: Its upper layers include the rigid lithosphere and the more plastic asthenosphere. For 10 points, name this largest layer of Earth, found between the crust and the core.

tossups.p: Rising columns of unusually hot rock called plumes move up through this layer and are thought to create volcanic hotspots far from the edges of tectonic plates, such as the one beneath Hawaii. This region’s convection also drives seafloor spreading at mid-ocean ridges.
tossups.r: Magnesium oxide and silicate minerals make up most of this hot, slowly flowing layer. For 10 points, name this plastic solid region of Earth’s interior that lies below the crust.

tossups.p: This layer makes up about 84 percent of Earth’s total volume, making it by far the largest of Earth’s main layers. Although made of solid rock, it flows extremely slowly over millions of years because of the heat and pressure deep inside the planet.
tossups.r: Convection currents in this layer drive the slow movement of the tectonic plates riding on top of it. For 10 points, name this thick layer of Earth found between the thin outer crust and the metal core.

tossups.p: This region’s uppermost, most rigid sliver combines with the crust to form the lithosphere, while just beneath that sits a softer, more easily deformed layer called the asthenosphere. Seismic waves slow down noticeably as they pass through this region’s low-velocity zone.
tossups.r: Scientists divide this huge rock layer into upper and lower portions, separated by changes in mineral structure under increasing pressure. For 10 points, name this layer of Earth that lies beneath the crust and above the outer core.

tossups.p: No drilling project, including Japan’s Chikyu Hakken expedition, has ever bored all the way down to this layer of Earth. The Mohorovičić discontinuity marks where this layer begins, just underneath the crust.
tossups.r: This thick layer of solid but slowly flowing rock surrounds Earth’s core. For 10 points, name this layer, the largest by volume inside the planet.

tossups.p: Within this region’s low-velocity zone beneath the continents, the Lehmann discontinuity marks a sudden increase in the speed of seismic waves. Far below, near this region’s boundary with the outer core, lies a distinct zone called D double-prime.
tossups.r: Heat escaping from deep inside the planet drives slow convection currents throughout this region. For 10 points, name this rocky layer of Earth found between the crust and the core.

tossups.p: Plumes of especially hot rock rising through this layer are blamed for volcanic hotspots that can appear in the middle of a tectonic plate rather than at its edge. Accounting for roughly 84 percent of Earth’s volume, this layer mostly behaves like a slowly flowing plastic solid.
tossups.r: This layer sits directly beneath the thin crust and directly above the molten outer core. For 10 points, name this huge middle layer of planet Earth.

tossups.p: Olivine is especially common in the upper part of this region, while scientists hypothesize that a mineral called post-perovskite forms near its lowest 200 kilometers. Magnesium oxide ranks as the second most abundant compound found throughout this layer.
tossups.r: This layer behaves like an extremely slow-moving fluid even though it is technically solid rock. For 10 points, name this layer of the Earth that lies beneath the crust and above the core.

tossups.p: The Gutenberg discontinuity marks the boundary between this layer and the liquid outer core, just below a zone called D double-prime. Convection within this layer is the main engine behind the movement of Earth’s tectonic plates.
tossups.r: This region makes up the bulk of Earth’s interior, sitting between the thin outer crust and the metallic core. For 10 points, name this huge rocky layer of the planet.

tossups.p: A low-velocity zone within the uppermost part of this layer sits just below a rigid cap called the lithosphere. Scientists aboard the Japanese ship Chikyu have tried to drill through the crust to directly sample rock from this layer.
tossups.r: Although solid, this layer flows slowly enough over millions of years to carry tectonic plates along on top of it. For 10 points, name this thick layer of Earth that lies beneath the crust.

tossups.p: This region begins just beneath the Mohorovičić discontinuity and ends at the Gutenberg discontinuity bordering the outer core. Near its very base lies the mysterious D double-prime zone, where seismic wave speeds change dramatically.
tossups.r: Slow convection currents inside this region are the main force behind the drifting of Earth’s tectonic plates. For 10 points, name this massive middle layer of planet Earth.

tossups.p: This layer of Earth lies directly below the crust and directly above the core, and it makes up the largest share of the planet’s volume. Although it is solid rock, heat from deep within the planet makes it flow slowly over millions of years.
tossups.r: Convection currents in this layer, home to the asthenosphere, drive the motion of tectonic plates on the surface above. For 10 points, name this thick rocky layer of planet Earth.

clues.t: Lies directly between Earth’s crust and its core, making up most of the planet’s volume
The largest layer in Earth by volume, making up roughly 84 percent of the planet
Technically solid rock, but it flows very slowly over millions of years like a thick liquid
Convection currents here drive the slow movement of Earth’s tectonic plates
Begins just below the crust at the boundary nicknamed the Moho discontinuity
Its soft, plastic upper part, the asthenosphere, flows more easily than the rock above or below it
Its rigid topmost sliver joins the crust to form the lithosphere
Rising plumes of hot rock create volcanic hotspots far from plate edges, like Hawaii
Its lowest part is a mysterious zone called D double-prime
An upper low-velocity zone slows seismic waves passing through it
Its convection also drives seafloor spreading at mid-ocean ridges
Divided into an upper portion and a lower portion, separated by changes in mineral structure under pressure
No drilling project, including Japan’s Chikyu Hakken, has ever bored all the way down to it
Its lower boundary with the outer core is called the Gutenberg discontinuity
The Lehmann discontinuity marks a sharp jump in wave speed within its low-velocity zone
A mineral called post-perovskite is hypothesized to exist near its very base
Its upper portion is especially rich in the green mineral olivine
Magnesium oxide is the second most abundant compound found throughout it
Made mostly of silicate rock rich in iron and magnesium
Partial melting here produces the magma that erupts as basalt at mid-ocean ridges
Pressure and temperature both increase gradually with depth, and so does density

trap.title: Whole mantle, or one part?
trap.body: The mantle has famous neighbors and famous parts, and a question can want any of them. The crust sits above it and the core sits below it, and both are completely different answer lines. Inside the mantle itself, the asthenosphere is only its soft, flowing upper part, and the Mohorovičić discontinuity (the Moho) is just the boundary where the mantle begins, not the whole layer.
trap.fix: If the clue describes the thin outermost layer we live on, say crust. If it describes Earth’s center, say core. If the clue is clearly naming just the flowing upper slice or the boundary itself, lead with that specific term — otherwise, for the big rock layer between crust and core, say mantle.
trap.line: Real answer line: Mantle [accept upper mantle or lower mantle; prompt on Mohorovičić discontinuity or asthenosphere]

topics.dates: About 1,500 potentially active ones exist on Earth today
topics.briefing: A volcano is an opening in Earth’s crust where molten rock, ash, and gas escape from deep underground. Mount Vesuvius buried the Roman city of Pompeii in ash in the year 79, and Krakatoa’s 1883 eruption was heard thousands of miles away. Most of them cluster along the Pacific Ring of Fire, where shifting tectonic plates give magma a path to the surface.

sample.note: the 8 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: NASA’s Dawn spacecraft found evidence that the dwarf planet Ceres may host an icy version of this kind of landform, one that releases cold, watery material instead of molten rock. Jupiter’s moon Io is covered in hundreds of active examples of this feature, which help give its surface a distinctive mottled color.
tossups.r: The largest known example in the solar system, Mars’s Olympus Mons, is a shield-type one of these that may still be active. For 10 points, name these geologic openings that erupt with lava, ash, and gas.

tossups.p: Eruptions from one of these structures can be classified as Plinian or Strombolian, depending on how explosive they are. Fast-moving, wet mudslides called lahars can rush down the sides of one of these features, which can also release a smooth, ropy kind of lava called pahoehoe [“pa-HOH-ay-HOH-ay”].
tossups.r: Underground pressure builds in a magma chamber until it bursts out of these structures, launching ash and rock called tephra. For 10 points, name these cone-shaped openings in Earth’s crust that erupt with lava.

tossups.p: Vertical pipes called diatremes and the bowl-shaped craters called maars can form near one of these structures. Consolidated ash from this kind of structure hardens into a rock called tuff, while cooling lava from it can become obsidian or pumice.
tossups.r: Shield and cinder-cone are two common shapes for this kind of structure. For 10 points, name these geologic structures that erupt with lava, ash, and gas from inside the Earth.

tossups.p: In the year 79, Mount Vesuvius buried the Roman city of Pompeii under ash during a catastrophic eruption. Centuries later, in 1980, the radio message “Vancouver, this is it” announced the start of a similarly destructive eruption from Mount St. Helens.
tossups.r: That 1980 eruption caused the largest landslide ever recorded. For 10 points, name these mountain-like openings in Earth’s crust from which lava and ash erupt.

tossups.p: Most of these structures form along the boundaries of tectonic plates, clustering heavily around the Pacific Ring of Fire. Away from plate edges, rising columns of hot mantle rock called plumes can still create one of these features at a hotspot, as beneath Hawaii’s Mauna Loa and Kilauea.
tossups.r: These structures release built-up pressure from underground magma chambers. For 10 points, name these mountain-like openings in Earth’s crust that erupt with lava, ash, and gas.

tossups.p: In 1883, the Indonesian island of Krakatoa produced one of the loudest eruptions in recorded history from one of these features, audible thousands of miles away. The Philippines’ Mayon is famous for its nearly perfect cone shape, a classic example of the steep-sided “strato” type of this structure.
tossups.r: These structures are found heavily around the Pacific Ring of Fire. For 10 points, name these openings in Earth’s crust through which lava, ash, and gas erupt.

tossups.p: A superheated mixture of gas and rock called a pyroclastic flow can race down the sides of one of these structures during a major eruption. A massive eruption from one of these features at what is now Yellowstone National Park left behind a giant caldera.
tossups.r: Lava from this kind of structure can cool into a natural glass called obsidian or a lightweight, bubbly rock called pumice. For 10 points, name these geologic features that erupt with molten rock.

tossups.p: Low-viscosity basalt flows can build a broad, gently sloped shield-type version of this structure, while thicker lava and ash build steeper cinder-cone and composite types. Hawaiian lava from this kind of structure can take the form of smooth pahoehoe or jagged a‘a [“AH-ah”].
tossups.r: These structures can also leave behind calderas after a particularly powerful eruption empties their magma chamber. For 10 points, name these geologic structures, including Mount Vesuvius and Mauna Loa, that erupt with lava.

tossups.p: Material launched from one of these structures during an explosive eruption is classified by size into ash, lapilli, and larger pyroclastic blocks, together called tephra. The Philippines’ Mayon, a steep strato-type example of this structure, is famous for its symmetrical cone.
tossups.r: The shield type of this structure instead forms from gently flowing basalt, as at Hawaii’s Mauna Loa. For 10 points, name these structures from which lava, ash, and gas erupt.

tossups.p: Named for the Hawaiian goddess of these features, Pele is an especially active example found on Jupiter’s moon Io. In our own solar system, the largest known example of this kind of structure, Mars’s Olympus Mons, formed from low-viscosity basalt flows into a broad shield shape.
tossups.r: On Earth, Hawaii’s Mauna Loa is a shield-type example of this kind of structure. For 10 points, name these geologic features that include a vent or rupture through which gas, ash, and lava erupt.

tossups.p: A sudden, explosive Plinian-type eruption from one of these structures can send a pyroclastic flow of superheated gas and ash racing down its slopes, while meltwater and ash can combine into a fast, deadly mudflow called a lahar.
tossups.r: Pressure builds inside an underground magma chamber until it finally escapes through this structure. For 10 points, name these cone-shaped geologic structures that erupt with lava and ash.

tossups.p: Vertical pipes called diatremes and the bowl-shaped craters that they leave behind, called maars, are both associated with this kind of structure. Ash expelled from one of these features can harden over time into a rock called tuff.
tossups.r: Cooling lava from this structure forms igneous rocks such as basalt, obsidian, and pumice. For 10 points, name these openings in Earth’s crust through which magma reaches the surface.

tossups.p: Most of these structures are found at the edges of tectonic plates, especially around the Pacific Ring of Fire, though some form instead over stationary hotspots far from any plate boundary. Hawaii’s chain of islands grew from exactly this kind of hotspot activity.
tossups.r: These structures can be shield-shaped, like Mauna Loa, or steep cinder cones. For 10 points, name these mountain-like structures that erupt with lava, ash, and gas from inside the Earth.

tossups.p: Mount Vesuvius famously destroyed the Roman city of Pompeii in the year 79 when ash and pyroclastic flows buried it. A massive ancient eruption from this kind of structure beneath what is now Yellowstone left behind one of the largest calderas on the continent.
tossups.r: These structures release pressure that builds inside underground magma chambers. For 10 points, name these openings in Earth’s crust that violently erupt with lava and ash.

tossups.p: These geologic structures form where magma from deep underground finds a path to Earth’s surface, often at the boundary between two tectonic plates. When pressure builds high enough inside an underground magma chamber, one of these structures can erupt, releasing lava, ash, and gas.
tossups.r: Famous examples include Mount Vesuvius in Italy and Mauna Loa in Hawaii. For 10 points, name these cone-shaped openings in Earth’s crust.

clues.t: An opening in Earth’s crust where magma, ash, and gas reach the surface
Erupts with lava, ash, and gas when pressure builds in an underground magma chamber
Comes in types like shield, cinder-cone, and composite, based on shape and lava type
Clusters heavily along the Pacific Ring of Fire, where tectonic plates meet
A fast-moving cloud of superheated gas and ash called a pyroclastic flow can race down its sides
A massive eruption can empty its magma chamber and leave behind a collapsed caldera
Meltwater mixing with ash can rush downhill as a fast, destructive mudflow called a lahar
Hawaiian-style lava can form smooth pahoehoe or jagged, chunky a‘a
Rock and ash launched into the air during an eruption are together called tephra
Can form away from plate boundaries at a hotspot, above a rising column of hot mantle rock called a plume
Explosive eruptions are classified by style, including Plinian and Strombolian types
Most form along the boundaries where tectonic plates meet
Cooling lava can harden into a natural glass called obsidian or a light, bubbly rock called pumice
Mars’s Olympus Mons, a giant shield-shaped example, is the largest known one in the solar system
Jupiter’s moon Io hosts hundreds of active examples, including one named Pele after the Hawaiian goddess
Evidence from NASA’s Dawn mission suggests the dwarf planet Ceres may host icy versions that release cold, watery material instead of molten rock
In the Philippines, Mayon is a steep, nearly perfectly conical strato-type example
Can leave behind vertical pipes called diatremes and bowl-shaped craters called maars
Consolidated ash from eruptions hardens over time into a rock called tuff
Mount Vesuvius buried the Roman city of Pompeii in ash in the year 79
The 1883 eruption of Indonesia’s Krakatoa produced one of the loudest sounds ever recorded
Hawaii’s Mauna Loa and Kilauea are both shield-type examples built from runny basalt lava

trap.title: Volcano, or volcanic eruption?
trap.body: Some real sets ask specifically about the event of erupting (“volcanic eruptions”) rather than the mountain-like structure itself (“volcanoes”), especially when the clues describe one historic disaster like Mount St. Helens in 1980. Both answers are accepted here, but a sharp player notices the difference: the landform sits there for centuries, while an eruption is one specific event.
trap.fix: If the clues describe one dramatic moment, like a famous radio message or a single landslide, lean toward “volcanic eruption.” If the clues describe the shape, parts, or general behavior of the mountain itself, say “volcano.” Also remember that magma is the molten rock before it reaches the surface and lava is the same rock afterward — neither word alone is the answer to “name this structure.”
trap.line: Real answer lines: Volcanoes [accept shield volcano, cinder-cone volcano, etc.] on most sets, and Volcanic eruptions [accept anything indicating volcanoes and erupting] on at least one real set — both accepted here

topics.name: Pangaea
topics.kicker: Ancient supercontinent · Broke apart into today’s continents
topics.dates: Formed ~335 million years ago; began splitting ~200 million years ago
topics.briefing: Imagine every continent on Earth squashed together into one giant landmass — that was Pangaea. About 335 million years ago, Earth’s continents collided into this single supercontinent, and scientist Alfred Wegener used its puzzle-piece coastlines and matching fossils to argue that the continents must once have been joined. Slow-moving plate tectonics tore Pangaea apart starting around 200 million years ago, splitting it into the continents we recognize today.

sample.note: the 5 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: This landmass’s assembly did not include the blocks that became Cathaysia, now part of China, and fossils of the reptile Lystrosaurus on several separate modern continents support its existence. The collision of Gondwana with Laurasia that assembled this landmass threw up the Appalachian Mountains.
tossups.r: Mesosaurus fossils found on both sides of the Atlantic Ocean offer more proof that this landmass once existed. For 10 points, name this ancient supercontinent proposed by Alfred Wegener, whose name means “all Earth.”

tossups.p: Rock layers in South Africa’s Karoo region match strata found across the Atlantic in Brazil’s Santa Catarina region, a clue cited as early evidence for this landmass’s existence. German scientist Alfred Wegener first proposed this landmass while developing his theory of continental drift, noting how the coastlines of South America and Africa seem to fit together like puzzle pieces.
tossups.r: This landmass was surrounded by a single giant ocean called Panthalassa. For 10 points, name this supercontinent that broke apart into today’s continents.

tossups.p: Fossils of the seed fern Glossopteris, found across several now-separated southern continents, helped convince scientists that this landmass once joined them together. A smaller sea named Tethys cut into this landmass’s eastern edge, separating its southern half from its northern half.
tossups.r: This landmass began splitting apart roughly 200 million years ago, first dividing into the northern Laurasia and the southern Gondwana. For 10 points, name this supercontinent that contained nearly all of Earth’s dry land.

tossups.p: Glacial scratches found in now-warm regions like southern Africa, South America, India, and Australia show that those lands once sat clustered near the South Pole as part of this landmass. Wegener’s 1915 book, _The Origin of Continents and Oceans_, used such climate clues alongside matching fossils to argue for this landmass’s past existence.
tossups.r: Scientists later confirmed this landmass had existed using paleomagnetism, the record of Earth’s magnetic field preserved in ancient rock. For 10 points, name this ancient supercontinent, the most recent single landmass to contain nearly all of Earth’s dry land.

tossups.p: This landmass is hypothesized to be only the most recent in a series of supercontinents that includes two earlier ones called Rodinia and Pannotia. Some geologists predict that continuing plate movement will eventually reassemble a similar future supercontinent, perhaps in another 200 million years.
tossups.r: This landmass’s formation left out a set of blocks called Cathaysia, now part of eastern Asia. For 10 points, name this supercontinent proposed by Alfred Wegener, whose breakup created the modern Atlantic Ocean.

tossups.p: Early in this landmass’s assembly, a collision between two large landmasses threw up a mountain chain that today appears as the Appalachians in North America, the Caledonides in Scotland and Scandinavia, and the Atlas range in Morocco. Those three ranges share matching rock layers even though they now sit on three separate continents.
tossups.r: This landmass broke apart starting in the Triassic and Jurassic periods, helping open up the modern Atlantic Ocean as the pieces drifted away from each other. For 10 points, name this most recent of Earth’s supercontinents.

tossups.p: An ocean called Panthalassa, meaning “all sea,” surrounded this landmass on every side, while the smaller Tethys Sea wrapped partway around its eastern edge. Mesosaurus, a small freshwater reptile unable to swim across oceans, left matching fossils on both the South American and African sides of the later Atlantic Ocean because of this landmass’s existence.
tossups.r: German meteorologist Alfred Wegener proposed this landmass’s existence as part of his theory of continental drift. For 10 points, name this ancient supercontinent whose name combines Greek words for “all” and “Earth.”

tossups.p: Fossils of Lystrosaurus, a stocky plant-eating reptile, have been found on modern-day Antarctica, Africa, and Asia, offering evidence for this landmass’s existence. Scratches left by ancient glaciers in regions that are now tropical, including parts of India and Australia, show those lands once sat much closer to the South Pole as part of this landmass.
tossups.r: Alfred Wegener first proposed this landmass in the early 20th century as part of his theory of continental drift. For 10 points, name this single enormous landmass that contained nearly all of Earth’s continents before it broke apart.

tossups.p: Fossils of the extinct seed fern Glossopteris appear across the southern continents that once made up this landmass’s larger half, a region later named Gondwana. This landmass’s puzzle-piece shape is visible today in how the eastern coast of South America curves to match the western coast of Africa.
tossups.r: This landmass formed roughly 335 million years ago as nearly all of Earth’s continents collided into one. For 10 points, name this supercontinent, a name combining the Greek words for “all” and “Earth.”

tossups.p: Rock strata in the Karoo region of South Africa line up with matching layers found across the Atlantic in Brazil, a clue early geologists used to argue that those regions were once joined as part of this landmass. A single world ocean named Panthalassa stretched around this landmass’s outer edge.
tossups.r: This landmass takes its name from Greek words meaning “all” and “Earth,” since it once contained virtually all of Earth’s land. For 10 points, name this supercontinent proposed by Alfred Wegener.

tossups.p: A now-extinct freshwater reptile called Mesosaurus left fossils on both the South American and African coastlines, even though it could never have swum across the ocean that now separates them. This landmass’s assembly closed up an earlier ocean through the collision of Gondwana and Laurasia, raising a mountain chain whose eroded remains include the Appalachians.
tossups.r: Alfred Wegener’s early 20th-century theory of continental drift first proposed that this landmass had existed. For 10 points, name this ancient supercontinent that broke apart into today’s continents.

tossups.p: Fossils of the seed fern Glossopteris and the reptile Lystrosaurus turn up in both Africa and the Indian subcontinent, lands now separated by a wide ocean, and were cited as evidence for this landmass. Alfred Wegener also noted how neatly South America’s eastern bulge fits against the western coast of Africa while developing his theory of continental drift.
tossups.r: This landmass eventually broke into the northern Laurasia and the southern Gondwana. For 10 points, name this ancient supercontinent.

tossups.p: This landmass is the most recent in a long line of supercontinents that includes Rodinia and Pannotia, part of a repeating pattern geologists call the supercontinent cycle. Scientists confirmed this landmass’s past existence partly through paleomagnetism, which reads the direction of Earth’s ancient magnetic field as it was frozen into cooling rock.
tossups.r: Alfred Wegener first proposed this landmass as part of his theory of continental drift in the early 1900s. For 10 points, name this supercontinent whose slow breakup eventually produced the Atlantic Ocean.

tossups.p: This landmass’s interior, far from any ocean, likely had an extremely dry, harsh climate with huge temperature swings between seasons. Its formation sealed shut an earlier ocean and sent up a mountain range whose worn-down remains now appear on three separate continents as the Appalachians, the Caledonides, and the Atlas Mountains.
tossups.r: A single world ocean called Panthalassa surrounded this landmass, while the smaller Tethys Sea bordered part of its eastern edge. For 10 points, name this ancient supercontinent that broke apart beginning around 200 million years ago.

tossups.p: Coal deposits found today beneath the ice of Antarctica suggest that continent once had a far warmer, swampier climate as part of this landmass, before drifting to its present polar position. This landmass did not include a set of continental blocks called Cathaysia, now part of eastern Asia.
tossups.r: This landmass formed around 335 million years ago, when nearly every one of Earth’s continents collided into a single mass. For 10 points, name this supercontinent, whose name combines the Greek words for “all” and “Earth.”

trap.title: Pangaea, Laurasia, or Gondwana?
trap.body: Quiz bowl also asks about Laurasia (the northern half Pangaea first split into) and Gondwana (the southern half) as their own separate answers. A tossup describing only Africa, South America, Antarctica, India, and Australia wants Gondwana. A tossup describing only North America, Europe, and most of Asia wants Laurasia, not the whole original supercontinent.
trap.fix: If the clues only cover the southern continents, it is probably Gondwana. If they only cover the northern continents, it is probably Laurasia. If the clues describe puzzle-piece coastlines, Alfred Wegener, or essentially all of Earth’s land joined together, it is Pangaea.
trap.line: Real answer line: Pangaea [one real set also accepted “Gondwanaland” on its earliest clues only; this site marks it wrong, since Gondwana is its own answer]

topics.name: Clouds
topics.kicker: Condensed water vapor in the sky · Types signal changing weather
topics.briefing: Clouds are visible clumps of water droplets or ice crystals floating in the sky, formed when rising water vapor cools and condenses around tiny bits of dust or pollen called condensation nuclei. Puffy cumulus clouds, flat sheet-like stratus clouds, wispy cirrus clouds, and towering storm-bringing cumulonimbus clouds are the main types. Clouds are a key stop in the water cycle, since the droplets inside them eventually fall back to Earth as rain or snow.

sample.note: the 9 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: Round or oval gaps called “fallstreak holes” sometimes appear within a layer of these, often linked to passing aircraft. The Bergeron process describes how ice crystals inside these grow at the expense of nearby liquid droplets, a key step in forming rain or snow.
tossups.r: Silver iodide can be used to artificially “seed” these, encouraging precipitation to fall. For 10 points, name these visible masses of condensed water droplets or ice crystals that float in the sky.

tossups.p: The lumpy, bulging underside pattern called “mammatus” often signals that a severe storm is brewing in these. Mountain-hugging “lenticular” versions of these, lens-shaped and sometimes mistaken for flying saucers, form when moist air is forced upward over a peak.
tossups.r: Silver iodide can be dropped from airplanes to “seed” these and encourage rain or snow. For 10 points, name these white or gray masses from which precipitation falls.

tossups.p: When these contain nitric acid, a rare iridescent type called “nacreous” can form in the bitter cold high above the poles, where it may contribute to ozone loss. A man-made “cirrus” type of these, called a contrail, streaks behind high-flying jet engines.
tossups.r: Towering “cumulonimbus” versions of these are nicknamed thunderheads and can flatten into an anvil shape during a storm. For 10 points, name these condensed groups of water droplets that form visible shapes in the sky.

tossups.p: A small cap version of these, called a “pileus,” can perch briefly atop a bigger, still-growing one below it. Jet-engine exhaust creates a man-made streak form of these called a contrail, and a colorful type found mainly near the poles, called “nacreous,” forms only in extreme cold.
tossups.r: In the water cycle, these form after evaporated water vapor rises and condenses. For 10 points, name these usually-white masses of water suspended in the sky, which include the stratus, cumulus, and cirrus types.

tossups.p: Some scientists have proposed spraying man-made, sulfate-based versions of these high in the atmosphere to help fight global warming, an idea discussed in the book _SuperFreakonomics_. Wispy streaks nicknamed “mares’ tails” and flat anvil-shaped tops describe two of the dramatic forms these can take.
tossups.r: Fog is simply a ground-level example of the stratus type of these. For 10 points, name these atmospheric masses of condensed water vapor, often described as white and fluffy.

tossups.p: Fallstreak holes, strange round gaps, can appear in a layer of these. A type of these found mainly near Earth’s poles, iridescent and formed only in extreme cold, is called “nacreous,” and jet-engine exhaust forms a man-made streak version of these called a contrail.
tossups.r: Stratus, cirrus, and cumulonimbus are common types of these. For 10 points, name these sky-borne masses of condensed water droplets.

tossups.p: These form when rising air cools below its dew point, the temperature at which water vapor must condense into liquid or ice. NASA’s Phoenix Mars Lander even spotted wispy, cirrus-like versions of these high in the thin atmosphere of Mars.
tossups.r: Most of these form in the troposphere, the lowest layer of Earth’s atmosphere. For 10 points, name these masses of condensed water that include the cumulus, stratus, and cirrus types.

tossups.p: English chemist Luke Howard introduced the Latin-based naming system for these in 1802, giving us terms like “cumulus” (meaning heap) and “stratus” (meaning layer). High, thin versions of these let sunlight in but trap outgoing heat, somewhat like a greenhouse gas.
tossups.r: Lower, thicker versions of these instead reflect sunlight back into space, cooling the planet. For 10 points, name these masses of condensed water vapor floating in Earth’s sky.

tossups.p: A tiny speck of dust, pollen, salt, or smoke called a condensation nucleus usually sits at the center of each droplet inside these. Round or oval “fallstreak holes” sometimes punch through a layer of these, and a lumpy, bulging pattern called “mammatus” on their underside often warns of a coming severe storm.
tossups.r: Silver iodide can be used to artificially “seed” these and encourage precipitation. For 10 points, name these visible masses of water droplets or ice crystals that float in the sky.

tossups.p: The Bergeron process, in which ice crystals grow faster than nearby liquid droplets, helps many of these release rain or snow. A rare, iridescent, polar type of these called “nacreous” can help deplete the ozone layer high in the stratosphere.
tossups.r: Contrails, the streaks left behind jet engines, are a human-made, cirrus-like version of these. For 10 points, name these condensed masses of water vapor that fill the sky.

tossups.p: Lens-shaped versions of these that hover near mountain peaks are sometimes mistaken for flying saucers. A lumpy “mammatus” pattern on the underside of a storm-bringing type of these usually signals severe weather is near, and a small “pileus” cap can briefly sit atop a fast-growing one.
tossups.r: These are a key part of the water cycle, forming once rising water vapor cools and condenses. For 10 points, name these masses of condensed water that include cumulus, stratus, cirrus, and cumulonimbus types.

tossups.p: Jet contrails are a man-made, cirrus-type example of these, and a rare iridescent polar type is called “nacreous.” Fallstreak holes occasionally punch round gaps through a layer of these, and the Bergeron process explains how ice crystals inside them can grow large enough to fall as snow.
tossups.r: Towering cumulonimbus versions of these are nicknamed “thunderheads.” For 10 points, name these condensed masses of water vapor, including the wispy cirrus and puffy cumulus types.

tossups.p: A fine-grained mist resting right at ground level is technically just a stratus-type example of these. High above, thin, wispy versions made of ice crystals can let sunlight through while trapping outgoing heat, somewhat like a blanket.
tossups.r: Puffy, cotton-ball-shaped versions of these are called cumulus, while flat, featureless sheets are called stratus. For 10 points, name these masses of condensed water floating in the sky, which turn dark and towering just before a storm.

tossups.p: These form around microscopic particles of dust, sea salt, or pollen called condensation nuclei, once rising air cools past its dew point. Scientists sometimes label the rare, colorful polar type of these “polar stratospheric,” since it forms unusually high in Earth’s atmosphere.
tossups.r: Seeding these with silver iodide can encourage more rain or snow to fall. For 10 points, name these visible masses of water suspended in the sky.

tossups.p: A hazy version of these resting right at ground level is just a stratus type with a different name. The towering, storm-bringing cumulonimbus type of these can flatten at its top into a wide anvil shape when it reaches the top of the troposphere.
tossups.r: These form through condensation, as rising water vapor cools past its dew point. For 10 points, name these masses of tiny water droplets or ice crystals that fill the sky.

topics.name: Limestone
topics.kicker: Calcium-carbonate sedimentary rock · Dissolves into caves, karst
topics.dates: Forms over millions of years in shallow seas
topics.briefing: Limestone is a sedimentary rock built mostly from calcium carbonate, often made of the crushed shells and skeletons of ancient marine creatures that piled up on old sea floors. Rainwater and weak acids slowly dissolve limestone underground, carving out caves, sinkholes, and dramatic landscapes called karst topography, complete with dripping stalactites and stalagmites. Builders have prized limestone for construction and cement for thousands of years, and heat and pressure underground can transform it into the smoother rock marble.
